items.q: Which buildings in central Berlin are original and which are rebuilt?
items.a: **Of the fourteen landmarks between the Staatsoper and Alexanderplatz, four are still original material: St. Mary's Church, the Neptune Fountain, the TV Tower and the World Clock.** The Rotes Rathaus, Zeughaus, Staatsoper, Altes Museum, Alte Nationalgalerie, Neues Museum and Berliner Dom are rebuilds that kept their original design and some original fabric. The Humboldt Forum and the Nikolaiviertel are reconstructions of buildings that had been completely removed.

items.q: What is the oldest building in Berlin?
items.a: **The Nikolaikirche, whose walls date from around 1230.** It stood as a roofless shell after 1945 and was rebuilt by East Germany between 1981 and 1987 on those original walls, so the lower brickwork is genuinely medieval while the roof and both spires are 1980s work. The oldest church still holding services is St. Mary's, built around 1270.

items.q: Is the Humboldt Forum a replica of the Berlin Palace?
items.a: **Three of its four outer faces are reconstructions of the baroque palace; the fourth is openly modern.** The original palace was begun in 1443, rebuilt into a baroque masterwork by Andreas Schlueter between 1698 and 1713, burnt in 1945 and blown up by the GDR in 1950. The building standing there now was constructed between 2013 and 2020. Walk around to the Spree side to see the point where the copying deliberately stops.

items.q: Did anything in central Berlin survive the Second World War?
items.a: **Yes, but less than the skyline suggests.** St. Mary's Church came through standing, and the Neptune Fountain survived because it is a free-standing monument. Most other landmarks survived as walls and shells: the Altes Museum, Alte Nationalgalerie and Berliner Dom kept a great deal of original stone, while their roofs, domes and interiors did not.

items.q: Is the Nikolaiviertel really Berlin's old town?
items.a: **No. It was built between 1981 and 1987 from standardised prefabricated concrete panels with historicising fronts,** under the architect Guenter Stahn, for the 750th anniversary of Berlin. The medieval street lines it follows are real and the Nikolaikirche in the middle has genuinely medieval walls, but almost every house around it is younger than the visitors photographing it.

items.q: Is the Quadriga on the Brandenburg Gate the original?
items.a: **No, it is a recast from 1957 and 1958.** Johann Gottfried Schadow's original of 1793 was wrecked in 1945 and destroyed in 1950. The replacement was made from a plaster model taken in 1942 and lifted into place on 1 August 1958. The gate underneath it, built between 1788 and 1791, is largely original stone restored between 1956 and 1958.

items.q: Why is the Berliner Dom shorter than it looks in old photographs?
items.a: **Because the reconstruction after the 1944 fire was deliberately simplified.** East Germany decided to rebuild in 1975 and finished in 1993. The dome and the four corner towers each came back sixteen metres lower than the originals, the small towers lost their lanterns, and the Memorial Church wing was never rebuilt at all.

items.q: Which Berlin building shows the difference between original and rebuilt best?
items.a: **The Neues Museum.** Finished in 1855, bombed, then left open to the weather for over fifty years. David Chipperfield's restoration ran from 1999 to 2009 and stabilised shell holes, scorched brick and half-lost murals instead of hiding them, setting them directly against plainly new plaster and concrete. You can put one hand on 1855 and the other on 2009 without moving your feet.
